## Electoral institutions, malapportionment and the representation of ethnic minorities

The representation of ethnic minorities in national legislatures varies enormously: in some countries minorities are privileged through reserved seats or territorial concentration, while in others they remain systematically excluded. *Electoral institutions, malapportionment and the representation of ethnic minorities* (Guinjoan, Mas &amp; Roura) asks how malapportionment itself shapes that variation — a mechanism that had received little comparative attention, largely because of the empirical difficulty of linking electoral outcomes to the territorial distribution of ethnic groups.

To close that gap, the paper introduces a novel cross-national dataset covering **more than 22,000 legislative districts in 84 countries (1996–2020)**, identifying for the first time, at the district level, the presence of ethnic minorities excluded from executive power.

### Headline findings

::::::: insight-grid
::: {.insight-card .surface-card}
<span class="insight-icon">🪑</span>

### Reserved seats, higher malapportionment

Countries that constitutionally reserve seats for ethnic minorities tend to exhibit **higher malapportionment** overall — the two tools go hand in hand.
:::

::: {.insight-card .surface-card}
<span class="insight-icon">📍</span>

### Minority districts are over-represented

Districts where ethnic minorities are territorially concentrated are **more often over-represented** than other districts — malapportionment working, deliberately or not, in minorities' favour.
:::

::: {.insight-card .surface-card}
<span class="insight-icon">🌍</span>

### Strongest where democracy is weakest

Minority over-representation is **most pronounced in open autocracies and weak democracies** — a pattern consistent with rulers using electoral rules strategically to manage ethnic cleavages rather than as a neutral by-product of geography.
:::
:::::::

These findings connect directly to REPBIAS's work on [electoral reform in authoritarian regimes](papers.qmd): the same territorial tools that can protect minorities can also be turned into instruments of strategic control.

:::
